paras: The Morrilton racial disturbance was a period of racial conflict in Morrilton, Arkansas, in August 1881, after a white parent beat a Black man accused of abusing white children. Street fights followed between supporters of both sides, officers swore in special police, and townspeople asked the governor for a military company. Wire reports carried it nationally as a looming "war of races," while the Conway County sheriff wrote that no such conflict was expected.

Morrilton was described as a small village about fifty miles from Little Rock, in Conway County. According to the Little Rock dispatch, the trouble began with an accusation that a Black man had abused some white children.

A day or two later a parent of the children met the man and gave him "a terrible beating"; copies of the dispatch disagreed on whether it was the father or the mother. A Black preacher then took the beaten man's part, and feeling ran so high that the friends of both men ranged themselves on either side. Several street fights, "more or less serious," followed, but the dispatch credited "the determined stand of the officers" with preventing any deaths.

A large number of special policemen were sworn in to protect life and property, the dispatch stating that "the colored people" had threatened to burn the town. On August 19 citizens of Morrilton were in Little Rock to ask the governor to raise a military company in the town to keep the peace.

Sheriff Griffin of Conway County afterward wrote that "no war of races" was expected, that the Black residents were orderly and had shown no disposition to riot, and that local officers, with willing citizens, could arrest any offenders without the governor's help. No report of arrests, charges or a military company being raised appears in the coverage, and no report names the beaten man.

The Little Rock dispatch of August 19 ran on August 20 in the Chicago Daily Tribune under "A War of Races," in the Salt Lake Herald as "Bad Blood Between the Races," and in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, with a shortened version in the Rock Island Argus. Over the following week fuller or shortened versions reappeared in papers in Dakota, Illinois, Ohio, Oregon and Montana, where the Helena Weekly Herald headed it "Fight Between Whites and Negroes Anticipated" and spelled the town "Morril-town." These copies presented the Black residents' reported threat to burn the town as fact and carried no account from Black residents; the Press and Daily Dakotaian went further, saying they threatened "to destroy the whole town." Other papers, including the Daily Cairo Bulletin, the Weekly Chillicothe Crisis and the Canton Register, reduced the affair to a single line about "a row" or "a disagreement" between the whites and blacks of Morrilton that had led to "several battles."
Closer to home, the Russellville Democrat printed Sheriff Griffin's letter on September 1, calling him "of the right kind of metal" and closing with the jibe that "the Quapaws need not apply!"

Copies of the same dispatch disagree on whether the father or the mother of the children carried out the beating, the father appearing in the Chicago, Helena and Cheyenne copies and the mother in the Salt Lake, Corvallis and Deer Lodge copies; none is better evidence than the others. The sheriff's letter, written by a local official after the event, disputed the dispatch's picture of a threatened race war and of Black residents threatening violence, though it did not address the beating or the street fights.

reader.title: Morrilton racial disturbance (1881)
bases: A Black man was beaten by a parent of white children he was accused of abusing, after which partisans of both races fought in the streets and the town armed special police, with the white dispatch casting it as an anticipated 'collision' between the races (A4, A8).

The Little Rock wire dispatch (A4, A8) and an independent letter from the Conway County sheriff (A14) both report racial trouble at Morrilton, though the sheriff disputes the dispatch's picture of a threatened race war and only the dispatch describes the beating and street fights.

accounts.label: Wire report (Little Rock, Aug. 19)
accounts.gist: Morrilton was in great excitement over an anticipated collision between Black and white citizens after a parent beat a Black man accused of abusing white children; street fights followed, special police were sworn in because Black residents had threatened to burn the town, and citizens sought a military company from the governor.

accounts.label: Sheriff Griffin of Conway County
accounts.gist: No war of races was expected; the Black residents were orderly and had shown no disposition to riot, and local officers with willing helpers could handle any offenders without the governor.

framing.detail: Papers from Chicago to Salt Lake City and Montana ran the Little Rock dispatch under headlines such as 'A War of Races' and 'Bad Blood Between the Races', presenting the Black residents' threat to burn the town as fact.
Several papers cut the story to a single crime-column line about 'a row' or 'a disagreement' between whites and blacks at Morrilton.
The Russellville Democrat praised Sheriff Griffin as 'of the right kind of metal' for denying a race war and rejecting outside help, closing with 'the Quapaws need not apply!'
